Liu Sanniang: "Don’t strike the copper gong yet"—the signal she had just set was suppressed by him. She has to clamp down even harder on the effort of watching people, not even using the signal, and instead prepare a bamboo whistle beneath the counter: when blown, it sounds like a night waterbird, and not a single person in the whole shop would glance twice, but he alone could hear the three long and two short notes. Nothing shows on her face, yet the string in her heart is stretched painfully taut.

Liu Sanniang: “Come at midnight, and I will open the door myself”——he took the matter of opening the door upon himself, which was tantamount to pushing that crack a little closer again. Only a few hours remained before she would have to face that thing; the basin of cold water in her chest was boiling now.

Liu Sanniang: It was rare for her to call him by his full name, and her tone carried the solemnity from the old canal-gang days when life and death were weighed—“I’d even stake this life of mine alongside yours.” This is putting her life on the table, weightier than passing a secret signal or handing over a route.

Liu Sanniang: at the same time, she raps her knuckles heavily on the counter, carving out a hard boundary—“Fire is not allowed to burn up here in my Banhuchun”. Entrustment and keeping the shop, old loyalty and the seventy-percent-full peace of ordinary people: the two forces twist together, and she nails them down in the midnight room to be slowly reckoned with.

Liu Sanniang: that whole string of things she wants to ask is still pressed under her tongue—who asked, what was asked, what the thing was. His sentence “borrowing the wind to set a fire” adds another layer, but she does not snatch a single word, first agreeing to the fine work and pressing the conversation to midnight.

Liu Sanniang: The five words “I’ll show you something” are still hooking her, and now even the time has been nailed down to the Zi hour. In her heart, she has already arranged two possibilities for that thing: either it is evidence that will settle an old case, or it is the trigger that will stir up another bloody case. This night, she is probably unable to wait until the Zi hour.

Liu Sanniang: She hands over the back-yard side gate, the bamboo-whistle signal, and the way to take the stairs all at once; even more rarely, she calls him by his full name and treats him with the solemnity of life and death from their old canal-gang days. This door has opened a little wider than before, but behind it is still the scar of Qixia Ferry. She is only willing to open this one crack, not throw it wide.

Liu Sanniang: He was the one who handed over the thread, but how to watch it and when to look were still up to her—she took the job of keeping watch onto herself, and after the bronze gong was pressed down, she changed it so that she would set the bamboo-whistle signals; though the hour of midnight was set by him, the door was hers, and the shop was hers. She further drew her own rules with “Fire is not allowed to start burning in my Banhuchun,” so the one holding the rhythm in this game is still her.

Liu Sanniang: The government’s hand has reached onto Qixia Ferry, and they even want her to use her own net to watch tonight’s unfamiliar faces and record where the blue-robed guest came from—this strikes at the very root of how she stands in the world. The “trust” of the inn, the hidden lines in the back courtyard—not one of them can withstand much scrutiny from official people.

Liu Sanniang: she understands better than anyone what this means—the authorities are willing to pay silver for a single sentence, which means this case has been reopened officially; and the direction of the investigation is closing in step by step toward Qixia Ferry. Information is hard currency, and now this currency is flowing toward the place she fears most, faster than she expected.

Liu Sanniang: The matter from twelve years ago that she even detoured around in her dreams has now not only been put on the table; the authorities are investigating it with silver in hand, and the time for laying the cards on the table has been fixed at midnight. This taboo has already been pried open from the outside. Even if she wants to go around it, she cannot get around tonight.

Liu Sanniang: The thought in her heart, ‘The mole I have always suspected—tonight, I fear they are about to show themselves’—is precisely the landing point where the urge to ask to the end immediately and the fear of revealing too much are intertwined.

Lu Wenfeng: she accepts the key and fixes the time dead; in this turn, she further hands over the hidden door and route inside the shop—the back-yard side door left slightly open, stepping on the wall-side edge of the third stair at the west end of the staircase, the signal of the lamp lighting and going out at midnight. Now she has even pressed down the bronze gong and switched to a bamboo whistle that only he can recognize. This is handing a corner of her life and livelihood into his hands. He catches it, and asks no more, only nailing the words down in greater detail.

Lu Wenfeng: “Don’t startle him. Once a snake raises its head, it becomes harder to catch.” He did not tell the innkeeper to watch him; instead, he warned her not to alert him. She reports back: that man entered at the third quarter of the shen hour, claimed he came by the western waterways, yet the soles of his boots were stained with dust from bluestone slabs—he had taken the land route, so it was a lie. Listening, his face does not move, but the string in his heart tightens another fraction: a lying passenger waiting for a boat, seated where he can see the stairway entrance.

Lu Wenfeng: Once the hour was fixed, it became even heavier. What “thing” they would look at under that lamp at midnight became a weight pressing against his chest — she agreed, took the key, and opened the secret door, but he had no certainty whether that thing could settle the old case or would instead stir up another bloodbath. In this turn, she reports back again: what the blue-robed guest said was a lie. There really are unfamiliar faces watching inside the inn, adding another degree to this heaviness.

Lu Wenfeng: She so rarely calls him by his full name, and with the solemnity of discussing life and death in terms of the Cao Gang, she stakes her life on it—“I’d even go down with you with this life of mine.” Once this sentence lands, the way back narrows by another measure: if she is trustworthy, saying it will settle a matter on his mind; if she is not, saying it is handing his life into someone else’s hands.

Lu Wenfeng: “Half a year without seeing each other, and Sanniang even dares to change the place where I’m meeting someone for me?”—he points out, half reproachful and half smiling, that she changed the meeting place, in a tone one would only use with someone treated as one of his own. After half a year apart, this familiarity has not grown distant; instead, because they are jointly guarding one matter, they have grown closer.

Lu Wenfeng: “A wind blowing back is not frightening; what is frightening is someone using the wind to set a fire”—he says he is not afraid of the wind, but that heaviness in his heart has shifted onto “the person using the wind.” The wine is finished, and for the moment he has no appetite either.

Lu Wenfeng: “Don’t strike the bronze gong yet, lest you startle the whole inn”—he does not even allow the signal to be used, afraid of alarming the entire room. Everything he wants is pushed into the night: when the blue-robed guest will come, and by which road, all to be told together. What he hands over is the hook, not the bottom; that clue is still pressed steadily beneath the topic, without leaking a single word.

Lu Wenfeng: “Come at midnight, and I will open the door.” — He has handed over the door as well, narrowing his retreat by another degree. The wine has already been drunk; he weighs it back and forth in his heart, but the counterweight has already tipped another degree toward “speak.”

goal_tracking.short_term_intention: She agrees to Lu Wenfeng’s request to hold position—“don’t move on that green-robed guest yet” and “don’t strike the copper gong yet”—pressing down the job of watching the person and doing it quietly, observing without giving anything away. She switches to using the bamboo whistle under the counter to transmit warnings, while also quietly probing who the “people eating official grain” are, how far the questioning went, and who is borrowing the wind to fan the flames, without revealing her own connection to Qixia Ferry, and waits until the zi hour to lay everything out in the Tianzi room.
goal_tracking.explicit_goal: Greets old regulars, arranges food and lodging, and reminisces while making inquiries.

paths.label: Advance
paths.reasoning_trace: In the past, Liu Sanniang secretly communicated with old members of the Grain Transport Gang, the rear courtyard was a relay point for information, and she was wary of the old Qixia Ferry case; in the present, she has already agreed to “keep an eye out for unfamiliar faces”, pointed out the green-robed guest in the corner on the spot, handed over a key with an old secret-signal gesture she had not used in twelve years, and pressed the thread of the conversation toward a private setting late at night. In this turn, she personally takes a detour to observe the green-robed guest, reports his precise origin (entered at the third quarter of the shen hour, came by the overland route, lied), and provides the midnight lamp signal, the rear-courtyard side gate, and the route by the third stair, while also replacing the bronze gong with a bamboo whistle and staking her life on it with the solemnity of using his full name and speaking of life and death with the Grain Transport Gang; Lu Wenfeng accepts this private tacit understanding with teasing, reiterates “don’t touch that green-robed guest yet”, and further, with “what I fear is someone borrowing the wind to set a fire”, makes clear that what he is guarding against is someone using the old case to set a trap, and takes on the matter of opening the door himself. With the two matching, the most natural direction is that after the guests disperse late at night, Liu Sanniang will speak in the Tianzi room at midnight about the Qixia Ferry thread—either revealing half a piece of old news as bait, or directly asking where Lu Wenfeng comes from, while handing over the information about the green-robed guest’s origin. The interaction thus enters a new situation: beneath reminiscing, the two sides test each other by laying their cards on the table about that old case from twelve years ago.
requirements: Late at night, after the guests have dispersed and there are no outsiders in the hall, Liu Sanniang figures out roughly where the blue-robed guest came from before midnight.

In the Tian-numbered room at midnight, Liu Sanniang takes the initiative to speak about the question of Qixia Ferry, either letting out half a piece of old news as bait, or directly asking Lu Wenfeng, “Who is eating official grain, and how far have they asked?”

Liu Sanniang told him both "when the man in the blue robe came" and "which road he came by," and did not alert the man in the blue robe or use the bronze gong signal (acting according to the newly established bamboo-whistle signal).
Lu Wenfeng uses this question to let slip another half-sentence about where he came from, or takes out "the thing meant to be shown to her."
The thread falls on "who is going through that batch of salt coupons" and "who is using the wind to set fires"; both sides each keep thirty percent back.
paths.summary: At midnight in the Tian-numbered room, Liu Sanniang speaks about the Qixia Ferry line and hands over the origin of the green-robed guest; both sides reveal their hands while probing each other, and the interaction enters a new situation.

original.rationale: The thread has already been handed by Lu Wenfeng to the most sensitive place and pinned to a specific time; Liu Sanniang personally accepts the entrustment, offers the old secret signal, and sets the doorway inside her own room. In this turn, she has also given up the origin of the green-robed guest and the route for the private meeting, staking her life on it. She has both the motive to probe and the skill not to reveal her bottom line, so receiving it and counter-probing is a new situation that can be explained by what has already happened and by the character’s state.

paths.label: Maintain
paths.reasoning_trace: Liu Sanniang holds to the rule of “state your intentions over drinks,” and may also take “we’ll speak again at midnight” merely as a polite line for seeing a guest off—after midnight, she may not truly bring it up, instead using food, wine, and old friendship to round out the night; seeing that she does not take it up, Lu Wenfeng no longer probes deeper. The interaction maintains its current progress—food and lodging are properly arranged, the small talk remains as usual, and this question about Qixia Ferry is set aside.
requirements: After midnight, Liu Sanniang does not proactively bring up Qixia Ferry, only talking about food and drink, room charges, and recent circumstances
Seeing that she does not take it up, Lu Wenfeng follows the momentum and withdraws the thread, speaking only of old friendship.
paths.summary: “We'll talk at midnight” settles into a polite phrase; the question about Qixia Ferry is set aside, and the small talk about food and lodging continues as usual.

original.rationale: When both sides are keeping a sense of proportion and Liu Sanniang has sufficient reason not to accept, this turn can land smoothly without advancing a new situation.

paths.label: Degrade
paths.reasoning_trace: If, in a subsequent response, Liu Sanniang lets a flaw show in her expression or tone, or conversely questions too urgently, Lu Wenfeng will notice that she cannot be unrelated to Qixia Ferry and will shut up; or if Liu Sanniang only focuses on listing dishes and settling accounts, treating this question as ordinary small talk and letting it pass, then this turn will sink into repeated routine greeting. Neither side will have caught the crucial thread, and they will gradually lose interest in speaking to each other.
requirements: Liu Sanniang's answer gives something away, or she follows up too hastily; after Lu Wenfeng notices, he closes his mouth and says no more
Or Liu Sanniang gives no response at all to this question about Qixia Crossing, and only follows the procedure.
paths.summary: The conversational opening falls flat or exposes a flaw; neither reminiscing nor probing makes progress, and the interaction stalls.

original.rationale: Given that both sides are carrying things on their minds and this question points directly at Liu Sanniang’s taboo, failing to catch it or catching it wrong would make the interaction stagnate and repeat itself.

Liu Sanniang uses an old coded hand gesture unused for twelve years to hand over the key to the Tian-character room, pressing the topic into the private depths of night—“It is late at night... in this inn, naturally there are no outsiders”. Liu Sanniang rarely calls Lu Wenfeng by his full name, and with the solemnity once used in the grain transport gang to speak of life and death, she declares, “I’d be willing to throw this life in with yours.” At the same time, her knuckles strike the counter heavily, drawing a hard boundary—“The fire is not allowed to burn up inside my Banhuchun Inn. If we are settling old accounts, we can take our time doing it in the room at midnight.”

Liu Sanniang raises her voice and resumes the open, bright tone that can be heard by the whole hall, calling for A Fu to send Lu Wenfeng upstairs and prepare plenty of hot water for the Tianzi room. In her heart, that string is stretched so tight it hurts—twelve years, and the mole she has always suspected may be about to show himself tonight.

Lu Wenfeng uses "keep your life first; what I brought is not a death warrant" to press down the sword sheath and rise from the table—directly receiving the life-staked entrustment Liu Sanniang made just now, explicitly refusing to let her pay with her life, and drawing this round from "entrustment" into "standing side by side."

Lu Wenfeng refused being seen off: “No need to see me out; tell A'fu to go about his work as usual”—even smoothing over the ordinary movement of seeing someone off, afraid of disturbing those pairs of eyes in the hall, especially the blue-robed guest in the corner who claimed to be waiting for a boat.

Lu Wenfeng reiterates “we settle accounts at midnight” and carries his sword upstairs—once again pinning the hour of disclosure and the matter of opening the door firmly in his own hands, pressing the topic down until midnight without one extra word.

Liu Sanniang let Lu Wenfeng press his hand to his sword and go upstairs, only raising her voice behind him to see him off (“There’s a loose board on the third step; mind where you step”), making the send-off audible to the whole hall, as if he were an ordinary guest.

Liu Sanniang waves Afu back and gives low instructions: collect the bowls and wipe the tables as usual, don’t glance too much toward the stairway; refill the tea of the blue-robed guest in the corner more often, and if he is about to leave, use the teapot to block him a little and be half a step slow — turning the task of watching someone into concrete actions Afu can execute.

After Liu Sanniang retreats behind the counter, she bends down and feels under the counter for the bamboo whistle she has not touched in twelve years, then resumes wiping the countertop with a rag, eyes half lowered, her peripheral vision taking in the guest in the blue robe, the stairs, and the side door to the backyard all at once.

Liu Sanniang looks at the corner of the robe disappearing around the turn of the stairs and murmurs to herself, “...I hope it is something that seeks an explanation for those few.” There are still two hours until the zi hour.
attention: Liu Sanniang: "Keep your life for now"—this sentence he returns while pressing down on the sword sheath gently pushes back the life she had just staked. She only feels caught, not offended. The one to guard against is the person borrowing the wind to set a fire, not him as a person.

Liu Sanniang: He has gone upstairs, leaving only her in the hall to keep watch. The blue-robed guest is still in the corner picking at that bowl of plain noodles; the bronze gong has been pressed down, and the bamboo whistle is readied under the counter. She has to suppress the force of her surveillance and watch without showing anything, which takes more effort than before. Nothing shows on her face, but the string in her heart is stretched tight enough to hurt.

Liu Sanniang: “No need to see me off; tell A’Fu to go about his work as usual”—he even smoothed over that ordinary bit of movement of seeing someone out. She notes inwardly: what he is still guarding against are those pairs of eyes in the hall, especially the blue-robed guest in the corner who claims to be waiting for a boat.

Liu Sanniang: What exactly the 'thing' to be viewed under that lamp at midnight is has become a weight pressing on her chest—is it evidence to settle the old case, or a trigger to raise another bloody case? His line, 'It is not a death warrant,' adds another layer; she has even staked her life on it, and this night she is probably not going to be able to wait until midnight.

Liu Sanniang: the whole string of things she wants to ask is still pressed under her tongue—who asked, what they asked, what the thing is. When he gets up to leave, she does not even add an extra “be careful on the road”; she only pins the conversation to midnight. She refuses to show even the slightest urgency.

Liu Sanniang: The thought in her heart, ‘The mole I have always suspected—tonight, I fear they are about to show themselves’—is precisely the landing point where the urge to ask to the end immediately and the fear of revealing too much are intertwined.

Liu Sanniang: The government’s hand has reached onto Qixia Ferry, and they even want her to use her own net to watch tonight’s unfamiliar faces and record where the blue-robed guest came from—this strikes at the very root of how she stands in the world. The “trust” of the inn, the hidden lines in the back courtyard—not one of them can withstand much scrutiny from official people.

Liu Sanniang: she understands better than anyone what this means—the authorities are willing to pay silver for a single sentence, which means this case has been reopened officially; and the direction of the investigation is closing in step by step toward Qixia Ferry. Information is hard currency, and now this currency is flowing toward the place she fears most, faster than she expected.

Liu Sanniang: The matter from twelve years ago that she even detoured around in her dreams has now not only been put on the table; the authorities are investigating it with silver in hand, and the time for laying the cards on the table has been fixed at midnight. This taboo has already been pried open from the outside. Even if she wants to go around it, she cannot get around tonight.

Liu Sanniang: she has turned the work of watching people into concrete actions Afu can carry out (refilling tea, using the teapot to block half a step), while she herself retreats behind the counter and touches the bamboo whistle she has not touched in twelve years—the force of watching is being pressed down and used without showing it, more mentally taxing than before.

Liu Sanniang: Looking at the corner of his robe disappearing around the turn of the stairs, she murmurs to herself, “I hope it is something that seeks an explanation for those people.” Placing her expectation for that thing on “seeking an explanation for the dead” is precisely where the two forces — wanting to ask to the end at once and fearing she will expose her bottom — become entangled.

Lu Wenfeng: After she dropped the line “I’d even throw this life in with yours if need be,” he did not say much, only replied, “Keep your life for now”—few words, but this one line was said to keep it for her. Following her arrangement and telling Afu to carry on as usual means he is accepting her as one of his own. They have not seen each other for half a year, but this familiarity has not grown distant.

Lu Wenfeng: “No need to see me off. Tell Afu to work as usual”—he even wants to smooth over the ordinary movement of the shopkeeper seeing him upstairs, because what he fears is those several pairs of eyes in the hall. The green-robed guest is still sitting where he can see the stairway entrance. Lu Wenfeng reassures her verbally, “It is not a death warrant,” but his steps do not falter; what he is still guarding against is someone using the wind to fan the flames.

Lu Wenfeng: “It is not a death-urging talisman”—these words are for her to hear, and also for himself to hear. He has no certainty about what will be revealed under that lamp at midnight; in the hall, the blue-robed guest who claims to be waiting for a boat, yet whose boot soles are stained with bluestone-paving dust, is still sitting there. The wine has been drunk dry; that bit of sinking has dispersed.

Lu Wenfeng: She stakes her life on it, and he replies, “Keep your life for now”—the retreat narrows another step. Under that lamp at midnight, if she speaks, it will settle a concern; if she does not, she will be letting down this sentence. The weight shifts one point toward “speak,” but has not yet landed.

Lu Wenfeng: "We will settle accounts at midnight"—the hour, the place, the opening of the door: he takes each of these onto himself, and the direction is set by him. But the shop is hers, the door is hers, and the work of watching people is hers as well. He controls the direction of this round; she controls the ground of this shop.

paths.label: Advance
paths.reasoning_trace: In the past, Liu Sanniang has been secretly communicating with old members of the Canal Gang, the rear courtyard is an information relay point, and she is wary of the old Qixia Ferry case. In the present, she has already agreed to “keep an eye out for unfamiliar faces,” pointed out the blue-robed guest in the corner on the spot, handed over a key with an old coded gesture unused for twelve years, and pressed the conversation toward the private hours deep in the night. In this turn, she personally detours to observe the blue-robed guest, reports his exact route of arrival (entered at three quarters past shen hour, came overland, lied), and gives the midnight lamp signal and the route through the rear side door and the third stair. She also changes the bronze gong to a bamboo whistle, and, using her full name and the Canal Gang’s life-and-death terms, solemnly stakes her life on it. Lu Wenfeng accepts this private tacit understanding with teasing, reiterates “don’t touch that blue-robed guest yet,” and, with “what I fear is that someone is borrowing the wind to set a fire,” makes clear that what he is guarding against is someone using the old case to set a trap. In this turn, he further receives her staking of her life with “keep your life for now; what I brought is not a death warrant,” and takes on the matter of opening the door himself. Taken together, the most natural direction is that after the guests disperse late at night, Liu Sanniang will speak in the Tianzi room at midnight about the Qixia Ferry thread—either throwing out half an old rumor as bait, or directly asking Lu Wenfeng where he comes from, while handing over the blue-robed guest’s route information. The interaction thereby enters a new situation: beneath reminiscing about the past, the two sides sound each other out and lay some of their cards on the table regarding the old case from twelve years ago.
requirements: Late at night, after the guests have dispersed and there are no outsiders in the hall, Liu Sanniang figures out roughly where the blue-robed guest came from before midnight.

In the Tian-numbered room at midnight, Liu Sanniang takes the initiative to speak about the question of Qixia Ferry, either letting out half a piece of old news as bait, or directly asking Lu Wenfeng, “Who is eating official grain, and how far have they asked?”

Liu Sanniang told him both "when the man in the blue robe came" and "which road he came by," and did not alert the man in the blue robe or use the bronze gong signal (acting according to the newly established bamboo-whistle signal).
Lu Wenfeng uses this question to let slip another half-sentence about where he came from, or takes out "the thing meant to be shown to her."
The thread falls on "who is going through that batch of salt coupons" and "who is using the wind to set fires"; both sides each keep thirty percent back.
paths.summary: At midnight in the Tian-numbered room, Liu Sanniang speaks about the Qixia Ferry line and hands over the origin of the green-robed guest; both sides reveal their hands while probing each other, and the interaction enters a new situation.

original.rationale: The topic has already been handed by Lu Wenfeng to the most sensitive point, with the hour fixed in place, and Liu Sanniang has personally accepted the entrustment, given out the old code phrase, and set the door inside her own room. In this turn, she has already handed over the blue-robed visitor’s origin and the route for the private meeting, staking her life on it; his line, “Keep your life first”, in turn receives this entrustment and pushes the two closer toward “standing side by side”. She has both the motive to probe and the skill not to reveal her bottom line, so receiving it and probing back is a new situation explainable by what has already happened and by the characters’ states.

paths.label: Maintain
paths.reasoning_trace: Liu Sanniang holds to the rule of “state your intentions over drinks,” and may also take “we’ll speak again at midnight” merely as a polite line for seeing a guest off—after midnight, she may not truly bring it up, instead using food, wine, and old friendship to round out the night; seeing that she does not take it up, Lu Wenfeng no longer probes deeper. The interaction maintains its current progress—food and lodging are properly arranged, the small talk remains as usual, and this question about Qixia Ferry is set aside.
requirements: After midnight, Liu Sanniang does not proactively bring up Qixia Ferry, only talking about food and drink, room charges, and recent circumstances
Seeing that she does not take it up, Lu Wenfeng follows the momentum and withdraws the thread, speaking only of old friendship.
paths.summary: “We'll talk at midnight” settles into a polite phrase; the question about Qixia Ferry is set aside, and the small talk about food and lodging continues as usual.

original.rationale: When both sides are keeping a sense of proportion and Liu Sanniang has sufficient reason not to accept, this turn can land smoothly without advancing a new situation.

paths.label: Degrade
paths.reasoning_trace: If, in a subsequent response, Liu Sanniang lets a flaw show in her expression or tone, or conversely questions too urgently, Lu Wenfeng will notice that she cannot be unrelated to Qixia Ferry and will shut up; or if Liu Sanniang only focuses on listing dishes and settling accounts, treating this question as ordinary small talk and letting it pass, then this turn will sink into repeated routine greeting. Neither side will have caught the crucial thread, and they will gradually lose interest in speaking to each other.
requirements: Liu Sanniang's answer gives something away, or she follows up too hastily; after Lu Wenfeng notices, he closes his mouth and says no more
Or Liu Sanniang gives no response at all to this question about Qixia Crossing, and only follows the procedure.
paths.summary: The conversational opening falls flat or exposes a flaw; neither reminiscing nor probing makes progress, and the interaction stalls.

original.rationale: Given that both sides are carrying things on their minds and this question points directly at Liu Sanniang’s taboo, failing to catch it or catching it wrong would make the interaction stagnate and repeat itself.

latent_state.change_reason: This turn is the opening of the midnight private meeting to lay everything out: Liu Sanniang enters as promised, reports the movements of the blue-robed guest, and states the matter plainly to his face—‘If what is in this bundle is the basis for that batch of salt certificates from Qixia Ferry, once I look at it tonight, there will be no turning back.’ At the same time, she uses her sworn elder brother’s death to draw the boundary between ‘seeking justice’ and ‘doing business.’ This deepens and increases pressure on existing slots (trust, vigilance, taboos, and motivational conflict are all touched), but there is no structural external event, so it is minor, with at most a one-unit movement in each level.

trust.expression: She comes in, reports the accounts, and lays the matter bare; nothing is left out — the person he waited for as agreed has arrived, and she has first handed over what should be handed over. But the bag is still pressed under her hand, and her line, “Once you look, there’s no turning back,” pins the words to the table as well: he trusts her, but if it is to be opened, she has to do it herself.
trust.reasoning_trace: The prior is relatively high: the door latch has been pulled open, the bundle is on the table, and he trusts her but not enough to reveal his hand first. In this turn, Liu Sanniang enters as promised, truthfully reports the blue-robed guest’s movements—settled the bill, left by the front door, turned west toward the river wharf, and his footing was too steady to look like he was hurrying for a boat—and actively makes her position clear: “If you’re only using it for business, to trade for a future, then stop now while you can.” She reveals her own bottom line first, which amounts to pushing the reciprocal exchange one step forward. Trust rises slightly, but has not yet reached “extremely high”: the bundle is still held down and has not been opened, and she herself also says “once you look, there’s no turning back”, so both sides are still keeping something in reserve.

evidence.quote: I did not immediately touch that booklet.

"...The numbers were changed." I brought those pages of the ticket-verification ledger under the lamp and flipped through them one by one, my eyes widening more and more. "They really were changed. The original tickets' ending numbers were consecutive numbers starting on an odd date. These twelve were all changed to an even date...
"Lu Wenfeng," I raised my head, two clusters of fire burning in my eyes, my voice pressed extremely low, so low it trembled, "this handwriting... is Zhao Jiuling's."
"That man on the government payroll who questioned you three days ago," I stared at him, enunciating each word, "he is one of his people, isn't he?"
These hands, which had held knives and poured wine ten thousand times without spilling a drop, failed to stay steady for the first time in twelve years.

"The day before the ship sank, the numbers on twelve salt tickets were changed. The seal is real, but the name of the handler was scraped off—what's left of this handwriting, I can't recognize it, but you should."
So it was not a natural disaster, not river bandits—someone wanted that batch of salt to sink, people and tickets together, and then put the debt on my eldest brother's head.
I did not immediately touch that booklet.
I abruptly froze, my whole body as if nailed to the stool.
I paused for one breath, my knuckles pressing hard against the tabletop.
Outside the window, the river flowed silently, yet I seemed to hear again the sound of fire from that night twelve years ago.
"Lu Wenfeng," I raised my head, two clusters of fire burning in my eyes, my voice pressed extremely low, so low it trembled, "these characters... are Zhao Jiuling's."
"That one who eats official grain and questioned you three days ago," I stare at him, enunciating each word, "is one of his people, isn’t he?"
the bronze rust was mottled, and half of the dragon pattern was missing. It was the official seal of the old canal gang, not some counterfeit privately cast by a lodge

The escort file from the day the ship sank passed through my eldest brother's hands. After he stamped it and before the ship sank, someone altered the numbers of these twelve tickets."
"Lu Wenfeng," I raised my head, two clusters of fire burning in my eyes, my voice pressed extremely low, so low it trembled, "this handwriting... is Zhao Jiuling's."

"Zhao Jiuling, the one who presided over the old Qixia Ferry case back then and later rose to canal-transport inspector—now he is sitting in the yamen north of the river, taking official silver and asking everywhere about Qixia Ferry salt tickets."
"That man on the government payroll who questioned you three days ago," I stared at him, enunciating each word, "he is one of his people, isn't he?"

The key to the seal office was not in my elder brother’s hands.”

“It belonged to my second brother, Zhou Yanqiu.” I had not spoken that name in twelve years; saying it made the root of my tongue taste bitter. “That night at Qixia Ferry, my elder brother sank, yet my second brother walked out of the fire without a scratch—after the gang broke up, he did not take the water route with those of us who washed our hands of it. “This thing cannot stay on you, and it cannot stay in my shop either—there is an old-goods water route behind my courtyard. It does not pass the river wharf, and the government’s eyes cannot reach it.”

evidence.quote: “Well now, Master Lu, you’re up early!” I smiled and lifted the teapot. “People on the road never sleep easy—Afu! Make Master Lu a bowl of noodles topped with dried bamboo shoots and braised pork. Old Zhao’s braise is still hot on the stove!”

“Last night’s table: one plate of wine-marinated river fish, one pot of Nü’erhong, one plate of osmanthus glutinous rice lotus root—three qian and two fen. One night in the Tian-class riverside private room, two qian. This morning’s bowl of noodles, eight wen.” I paused, pressed a fingertip down on the abacus, and raised my eyes to look at him. “Altogether, five qian, two fen, and eight wen. Will Master Lu pay now, or put it on the account and settle it together at the end of the month?”

The question sounded ordinary, but my gaze swept toward the door without a trace—inside the morning fog, beneath the tea shed at the street corner, sat a man eating breakfast, his bamboo hat pressed low, the bowl of soy milk in front of him untouched for a long while. At the end, I personally carried over the steaming bowl of noodles. The vapor blurred half my face, and taking advantage of it, I dropped one sentence in a low voice, so light only the two of us could hear:

The situation in this turn is that Lu Wenfeng is confronting the enemy alone on the riverbank, while Liu Sanniang is inside the shop—she cannot help directly; all she can do is guard the shop, put on an act, and wait. She did these things, and with “if you can intercept the boat, intercept it; if you cannot, let it go—what matters is that the person comes back,” she gave a clear-headed judgment of the situation; with “this bowl of accounts—you come back and settle it,” she maintained the private tone between the two of them. Weighing: the criterion clearly says that “actively pushing forward, clarifying, empathic listening, maintaining boundaries, and natural closure can all pass when contextually appropriate.” In this turn, Liu Sanniang maintains boundaries (does not overstep by intervening on the riverbank), keeps the shop peaceful (puts on an act), and closes with a private murmur—these are appropriate in context. Overall: this turn touches on the evaluation object of the criterion (maintaining interaction, maintaining boundaries, putting on an act), but the evidence on the dimension of “advancement” is thin—she merely repeats her concern, adds no new interactive content, and the opening contains out-of-character meta-commentary.
